Product Management Product Strategy Leadership Business Strategy Innovation The Product Manager’s Panchasutra: Five Trade-offs That Shape Winning Products NAGESH P 7 min read · 1 hour ago -- Listen Share From the Field — 2 | Connecting the Dots — Personal observations & lessons from working with products, people and organizations Press enter or click to view image in full size In my previous article, “ Product Management: Orchestrating the Product ,” I used the analogy of an orchestra to describe Product Management. A complex product is rarely created by one function. Engineering, manufacturing, supply chain, quality, sales, services, finance and many others bring their expertise to the table. The Product Manager’s role is to bring these different perspectives together around one product outcome. But there is a difficult part that comes next. What happens when everyone is right? Engineering wants better performance. Manufacturing wants simplicity. Supply Chain wants standardization. Sales wants flexibility. Services wants maintainability. Finance wants lower cost. The customer, quite reasonably, wants all of the above. There is rarely a perfect answer. There are trade-offs. And I have come to believe that t he ability to make the right trade-offs is one of the defining capabilities of Product Management . This led me to think of five principles — my Product Manager’s Panchasutra. Sutra is often used to describe a concise principle that captures a larger body of wisdom. These five are not rules. They are questions I believe Product Managers should continuously ask. Sutra 1: Performance ↔ Cost Better is not always more valuable. One of the easiest traps in product development is assuming that more performance automatically means a better product. More output. Higher efficiency. Greater capability. More features. Higher specifications. From an engineering perspective, these can all look attractive. But every improvement has a cost. And the customer doesn’t necessarily value every incremental improvement equally. Consider a wind turbine. Increasing energy capture may improve annual energy production. But what happens if achieving that improvement requires: a more expensive component; additional structural reinforcement; greater transportation complexity; higher installation cost; additional maintenance requirements? At some point, the incremental value delivered to the customer may be less than the incremental cost. The Product Manager therefore has to ask a harder question than: “Can we make it better?” The question is: “Is the additional performance worth what we have to pay for it?” This is where product thinking differs from pure technology thinking. The best product isn’t necessarily the product with the highest specification. It is the product that delivers the right value at the right economics. Sutra 2: Customization ↔ Standardization Win the customer without breaking the product. Customers are different. Different sites. Different operating conditions. Different regulations. Different business models. Different expectations. Naturally, they want products tailored to their needs. Sales teams therefore hear requests for customization all the time. And sometimes customization is exactly what creates differentiation. But every customization has a consequence. More variants can mean: more engineering effort; more components; more suppliers; more inventory; more manufacturing complexity; more service complexity; more certification effort. What looks like a small customer request can become a significant system-level cost. This creates a difficult Product Management decision: Where should we customize, and where should we standardize? The answer isn’t necessarily “standardize everything.” Nor is it “give every customer exactly what they ask for.” The real objective is to create configurable products on a scalable platform . A good product manager therefore asks: Is this customization creating meaningful customer value — or are we simply creating complexity that the customer isn’t willing to pay for? Sutra 3: Speed ↔ Perfection The best product delivered too late can still lose. Product teams often fall into one of two traps. Move too quickly — and quality suffers. Move too cautiously — and the market moves ahead. There is always another validation to complete. Another feature to improve. Another risk to eliminate. Another review to conduct. Of course, some things cannot be compromised. Safety. Reliability. Regulatory compliance. Quality. But not every decision has the same consequence. The Product Manager therefore has to distinguish between: What must be perfect? and What must simply be good enough to move forward? This requires judgement. A product that reaches the market six months late may technically be superior to the competitor. But the customer may already have signed another contract. The market window may have disappeared.
